clue.text: Indian dish female relative brought up, we hear

parts.note: a nan is a grandmother, a female relative

indicators.note: 'we hear' says the words are to be taken by their sound when spoken, not their spelling

parts.note: brought up as a child means bred, which sounds the same as the baked staple

explanation.surface: A curry-house memory: some Indian dish that an aunt or grandmother made while you were growing up, or so the family says.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second half changes spelling: 'brought up' is BRED, and saying it gives the flatbread's second word. NAN is British informal for a grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: Naan bread is the leavened flatbread baked in a tandoor and served with curries across the subcontinent.

clue.text: Church body welcome after November

indicators.note: 'after' puts the greeting behind the radio letter, fixing the order of the two parts

parts.note: N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet
ave is a Latin greeting, hail or welcome

explanation.surface: A congregation or church committee greeting newcomers once November arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church body' reads as a governing group of people; here it is the physical body of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: The nave is the main central hall of a church building, where the congregation sits, as opposed to chancel or aisles.

clue.text: Connect canapé with cooking rejection

indicators.note: cooking mixes and transforms ingredients, so the letters of the two food-and-link words get stirred up

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
taken letter for letter as fodder, the accent dropped

explanation.surface: Party-kitchen instructions: pair something with the canapés while cooking, then a flat refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: The thirteen letters of the first two words together make the answer exactly; 'with' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing to take or agree to something is non-acceptance, a plain synonym for turning it down.

clue.text: Protest concerning giant almost consuming rodent

indicators.note: to consume is to take inside, so the shortened giant swallows the rodent
'almost' means not quite all, so the giant loses its final letter

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in a memo heading
a monster is a giant creature
a rat is a rodent

explanation.surface: A demonstration against something about a huge beast eating a rat, like a creature-feature complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protest' could be a noun, but the answer is the verb; 'almost' takes only the giant's last letter, and the rodent goes in just before where it stood.
explanation.definitionFit: To remonstrate is to object forcefully or make a protest, so the verb fits as a synonym.

clue.text: Aviator with tune descending on isle

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming down on top of something places the tune above the island

parts.note: an air is a melody or tune
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A pilot humming a tune while coming in to land on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Descending' is the flight picture, but here it only places one part on top of the other in the column. The Isle of Man is a British Crown dependency.
explanation.definitionFit: An airman is someone who flies aircraft, especially in an air force, the same as an aviator.

clue.text: Politician flanked by two African warriors

indicators.note: to be flanked is to have something on either side, so the two ones sit around the politician

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals
MP is Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician escorted by a pair of African warriors, like bodyguards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two African' wants to be read together; 'two' is the Roman numeral, split round MP.
explanation.definitionFit: An impi is a regiment or armed band of Zulu fighters, so the word names a group of warriors from southern Africa.

clue.text: US state's religious service: a church employs outside toilet (empty)

indicators.note: 'employs outside' puts the verb around what follows, so it wraps the emptied toilet

parts.note: Mass is the Catholic eucharistic service
taken as it stands
CH is the standard abbreviation for church
to employ something is to use it

indicators.note: an empty toilet has had its insides removed, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: only the outside letters of the word survive

explanation.surface: An odd newspaper line about a New England service where a church has use of an outdoor toilet that is standing empty.
explanation.walkthrough: The emptied toilet sits inside the verb between its last two letters; 'employs' is a verb in the surface and simply a word to be split here.
explanation.definitionFit: Massachusetts is one of the six New England states of the USA, capital Boston.

clue.text: Sort of ballerinas' ensemble, somewhat reduced

indicators.note: cutting the phrase down at both ends leaves only a portion of the dancers' words

parts.note: the run starts inside the dancers and ends inside the group

explanation.surface: A ballet company's corps looking a bit thinner than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like the start of a description of the troupe, but it is the definition, meaning partly or in some way.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases hedge a statement, meaning partly true or in some respects, so they swap freely in speech.

clue.text: Leave no mark, concealing poison

indicators.note: the opening words conceal the answer, holding it tucked inside their letters

parts.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and ends at the start of the third

explanation.surface: Advice to a poisoner: hide the poison so it leaves no trace on the victim.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Leave no mark' look like a complete instruction, when it is only the container for the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Venom is the toxic fluid snakes and spiders inject, a kind of natural toxin.

clue.text: Freezing water affected ears: SOS!

indicators.note: things that are affected are altered, so the letters are changed round

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A cold-water swimmer calls for help after icy water gets into the ears.
explanation.walkthrough: The distress call is just three letters of fodder, added to the ears.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ross Sea is a deep bay of the Southern Ocean off Antarctica, icy and often frozen over.

clue.text: Making last point in sung composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together from parts, so the letters are rearranged into a new word

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A composer making a final point in a sung piece, the closing phrase of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making last' reads as putting something in last place; here 'last' is the verb meaning endure, and 'in' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin something out is to prolong it or make it go further, such as stretching money or a story.

clue.text: Corrupt Conservative with old African dictator in art gallery

parts.note: Con is the short form of Conservative in British politics

indicators.note: the dictator is placed inside the gallery's name, splitting it after its first letter

parts.note: the Tate is the national gallery group in London
Idi Amin ruled Uganda in the 1970s

explanation.surface: A scandal: a corrupt Tory politician and a notorious dictator turning up together in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like an adjective describing the Conservative, but it is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To contaminate is to pollute or spoil the purity of something, the verb sense of corrupt.

clue.text: Colonel, old doctor and I going to a S American country

parts.note: Col is the military abbreviation for Colonel
O is a common abbreviation for old
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a medical degree
taken as it stands
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A travel party of an army officer, a retired physician and the narrator heading off to South America.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'a' is part of the wordplay, not an article before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Colombia is a republic in the north-west of South America, with Bogotá as its capital.

clue.text: Furious at Rome's conspiracy of silence

indicators.note: something furious is wild and agitated, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone angry at the Italian capital for its code of keeping quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian setting fits: the answer is the Mafia's code, and its letters are right there in 'at Rome'.
explanation.definitionFit: Omertà is the Mafia code forbidding anyone to talk to the authorities, a sworn rule of keeping quiet.

clue.text: Gradually moves a very short distance

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: creeps forward a little at a time

definitions.note: singular phrase for the plural noun, as in 'missed by inches'
definitions.meaning: the noun sense: tiny units of length, a narrow margin

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about slow motion; split it after 'moves' to get a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch is to creep forward slowly, and inches are tiny imperial units of length, idiomatically a narrow margin.

clue.text: Pleasant new English description of a creed

parts.note: nice means pleasant
N is the abbreviation for new
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A pleasant, fresh English-language summary of a statement of faith.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjective phrase: the word is the name attached to a particular creed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nicene Creed, from the Council of Nicaea in 325, is the Christian statement of belief recited in many churches.

clue.text: Cases not kept in a set-top unit, unusually

indicators.note: 'unusually' means in an out-of-the-ordinary way, so the letters are set in an unfamiliar order

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter as fodder, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Some cases, like DVD boxes, left out of the cabinet under the TV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' looks like containers for discs; in hospital terms a case is a patient, and these are not admitted overnight.
explanation.definitionFit: Outpatients are hospital patients treated without staying on a ward, so they are cases not admitted as residents.

clue.text: Architect's flyer

definitions.meaning: Sir Christopher, who designed St Paul's Cathedral

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral in London; the flyer is the tiny brown songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word is the surname of a famous English building designer and the name of a small bird.

clue.text: Flammable substance that's existed around New Zealand, close to wildlife

indicators.note: 'existed' goes around the country's code, holding it inside

parts.note: has been means has existed
NZ is the standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter of 'wildlife' is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fire-risk chemical long present in New Zealand, dangerously near its wildlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Existed' is the past participle here, as in 'has been', and it is split in the middle to hold the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Benzene is a volatile aromatic hydrocarbon liquid that catches fire easily, used as an industrial solvent.

clue.text: Swimmer in fur coat, much warmer, losing head!

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is dropped here

parts.note: much warmer is hotter

explanation.surface: A bather in a fur coat getting far too warm and losing their head over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer in fur coat' sounds like a person overdressed for a dip; it is an animal whose own fur is its coat.
explanation.definitionFit: An otter is a semi-aquatic mammal with thick waterproof pelt that spends much of its life in rivers.

clue.text: Several are flying each week, first of all

indicators.note: 'first of all' asks for the first letter of every one of the preceding words

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A handful of planes or birds take off every week, before anything else happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of all' reads as 'to begin with'; here it means the first letter of all the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Several and a few both mean a small number, more than two but not many, so they swap directly.

clue.text: Abandon plane? No, lie back!

parts.note: a jet is an aircraft

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the refusal and the verb read right to left

parts.note: taken as it stands
to sit is to lie or rest in position, as a building sits on a hill

explanation.surface: A pilot told to bail out refusing, and just lying back in the seat instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandon plane?' sounds like bailing out; 'Abandon' alone is the definition. Only 'No, lie' is turned round; the plane goes in front untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: To jettison is to throw away or discard something, such as cargo from a ship or aircraft, hence give it up.
